title: Lourdes
hookLine: the spring, the sick, and a medical bureau that investigates claimed cures

lines: WATER FROM A GROTTO IN FRANCE.
AND AN OFFICE FULL OF DOCTORS.
cards: On a kitchen shelf sits a small plastic bottle shaped like Mary, with a blue cap for a crown. Somebody's aunt brought it home from France, filled from a row of taps by a river. Nobody drinks it casually.
It gets a drop on a sick child's forehead, or a sip before surgery. The water comes from a spring in a grotto at Lourdes, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, and it draws the sick from far away.
And beside the grotto is something you might not expect at a shrine: an office full of doctors whose job is to be skeptical.

teach.b: You met Bernadette at this grotto back in year one.
First, the spring. Tradition says the lady told Bernadette to drink from the spring and wash in it, and there was no spring, only mud. She dug with her hands, and the water came.
Water and washing matter in the Gospels too. Jesus puts clay on the eyes of a man born blind and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloe." The man washes and comes back seeing.
Lourdes stands in that line. Second, who goes first. At Lourdes the sick aren't kept out of sight.
Volunteers push their wheelchairs and stretchers to the front of the processions, to the baths, to the grotto. The people the world hurries past are guests of honor.
Third, the doctors. When someone claims a cure, the shrine's medical office examines it. Was the illness real and serious?
Was the cure sudden, complete and lasting? Can medicine explain it? Only if a cure passes all of that does it go to the healed person's own bishop, who decides whether to call it a miracle.
The bar is high, and the process slow. Fourth, the water itself.
The shrine says it's ordinary spring water.

teach.h: GO, WASH IN THE POOL OF SILOE.
teach.b: Catholics treat it as a sign: of washing, of trust, of asking. Sick pilgrims can go home no better in body.
Some say they came back changed anyway, less alone and less afraid, and they return to push someone else's wheelchair.

how: Catholics make pilgrimages to the grotto at Lourdes, where the sick are given the first place in processions, pilgrims drink and wash in the spring water, and a medical office examines reported cures before any bishop judges them.

games.q: you're a doctor in the medical office at Lourdes. a pilgrim says she walked out of the baths without her crutches. what do you do?
o: announce a miracle the same day.
examine her records and wait to see if the cure lasts.
send her home; cures don't happen.
games.why: the office asks whether the illness was real and serious, whether the cure was sudden, complete and lasting, and whether medicine can explain it. only then does a bishop decide.

practice: Picture the grotto at night: candles, a long line of wheelchairs, volunteers leaning on the handles. Bring in one sick person you know by name, set them in that line near the front, and stay with them a while.
If you pray, say a Hail Mary for the sick at Lourdes and for them; if not, simply keep them company in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Lourdes. The French town where a spring rises in a grotto, the sick go first, and doctors test every claimed cure before a bishop will call it a miracle. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the waters. Ordinary spring water, carried home as a sign. See you tomorrow.
